title: Most Distant Quasar Found 630 Million Years After Big Bang
byline: Elias Reed Published: Nov 24 2026, 10:34 AM EST
excerpt: Astronomers using Euclid and Webb have confirmed the most distant quasar yet, J1504+6252, powered by a black hole several hundred million times the Sun’s mass.
content:
Astronomers have confirmed the most distant quasar ever found, a blazing object powered by a supermassive black hole that already weighed several hundred million times as much as the Sun just 630 million years after the Big Bang.

The quasar, named J1504+6252 and nicknamed Dún Aonghasa by the team, was first spotted by the European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope and confirmed with the James Webb Space Telescope, according to a release from the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy (MPIA). It has a redshift of 8.13, making it the first quasar found beyond a redshift of 8.

The research, led by Julien Wolf, is published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics, Popular Science reported. The discovery puts tighter limits on how the first giant black holes could have formed.

What a quasar is

A quasar is the brilliant core of a galaxy in which a supermassive black hole is feeding on large amounts of gas. As gas spirals toward the black hole, it heats up and glows so intensely that a quasar can outshine all the stars in its galaxy. That brightness lets astronomers see quasars across enormous distances.

Because light takes time to travel, looking at very distant objects means looking back in time. Light from J1504+6252 left it when the universe was about 630 million years old, less than 5% of its current age of about 13.8 billion years.

How it was found

The quasar was first identified in the Euclid Wide Survey, Euclid's large map of the sky, according to MPIA. Euclid, launched in 2023, is designed mainly to study dark energy and dark matter, but its wide, sharp, infrared view also makes it an efficient hunter of distant quasars.

Follow-up observations then built the case step by step. The W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaiʻi and the Hubble Space Telescope provided the first hints, MPIA said. The Large Binocular Telescope in Arizona and finally the James Webb Space Telescope revealed the precise redshift of 8.13.

Redshift measures how much an object's light has been stretched to longer, redder wavelengths by the expansion of the universe. The higher the redshift, the farther away and further back in time the object is.

Breaking Euclid's own record

The discovery follows a run of records. Earlier in 2026, a team using Euclid announced 31 new distant quasars, including one at a redshift of about 7.77 that was then the most distant known, according to the study in Astronomy & Astrophysics. Dún Aonghasa existed about 40 million years earlier than the previous record holder, MPIA said.

Popular Science reported that the new quasar was found in about 18 months of Euclid data, among millions of objects. Its nickname, Dún Aonghasa, comes from a prehistoric stone fort on the Aran Islands of Ireland.

Why it is a puzzle

The main mystery is speed. How could a black hole grow to hundreds of millions of solar masses in such a short time after the Big Bang?

Black holes grow by swallowing gas, but there is a natural limit to how fast they can do so, called the Eddington limit. As gas falls in and heats up, it shines so brightly that the pressure of the light pushes other gas away, slowing further growth.

According to MPIA, J1504+6252 is currently growing far below that limit. If it had always grown that slowly, it would have needed an implausibly massive "seed" black hole at the start. Its existing mass instead suggests it grew faster in the past, possibly even above the Eddington limit for a time.

"The closer to the Big Bang we find them, the faster their black holes must have grown," Wolf said, "or the more massive they must have been at birth, or both."

Clues to how black holes are born

Scientists have proposed several ways the first black holes could have formed. In one, called "light seeds," the first black holes were the remains of early massive stars, only tens or hundreds of times the Sun's mass. In another, called "direct collapse," a large cloud of gas collapsed straight into a black hole perhaps tens of thousands of times the Sun's mass, giving it a big head start.

Using reasonable growth rates, the team found the quasar is consistent with the direct-collapse scenario, MPIA said. The conditions needed for direct collapse were probably rare at this early time, which could explain why so few quasars have been found beyond a redshift of 7.5.

If even more distant quasars are found in future, direct collapse may struggle to explain them. In that case, scientists may need to consider more exotic options such as primordial black holes, hypothetical black holes that might have formed in the first moments after the Big Bang.

Limits of the finding

The black hole's mass is an estimate based on the quasar's light, and such estimates carry uncertainties. Different methods can give somewhat different values. The team's conclusions about growth also depend on assumptions about how fast black holes can feed over time.

A single quasar cannot settle the question of how black holes form. What it does is narrow the possibilities, and future discoveries will test them further.

How the distance is measured

Astronomers measure a quasar's redshift by spreading its light into a spectrum, a rainbow of wavelengths, and looking for known features. One key feature in very distant quasars is a sharp drop in light at a particular wavelength, caused by hydrogen gas between us and the quasar absorbing light. By finding where that drop appears, astronomers can calculate how much the light has been stretched.

At a redshift of 8.13, light that left the quasar as ultraviolet arrives at Earth as infrared. That is why infrared telescopes such as Euclid and Webb are essential for finding and confirming the most distant quasars.

Euclid's bigger mission

Euclid was launched in July 2023 to map a large fraction of the sky and study the mysterious dark energy and dark matter that shape the universe. Quasar discoveries are a valuable bonus. Because Euclid scans huge areas with sharp infrared vision, it can pick out rare, faint objects that smaller surveys would miss.

The finding also matters for understanding galaxies. Supermassive black holes and their host galaxies appear to grow together, influencing each other through gas flows and energy released by the black hole. Studying early quasars like J1504+6252 helps astronomers learn how the first large galaxies formed around them.

What comes next

Euclid's survey is far from finished. As it maps more of the sky, astronomers expect to find more distant quasars, possibly some even farther away than J1504+6252. Webb will remain essential for confirming them and studying their host galaxies in detail.

Each new record pushes our view of the early universe a little closer to the cosmic dawn, when the first stars, galaxies and black holes were taking shape.

Key Questions Answered

What is the most distant quasar found so far?

J1504+6252, nicknamed Dún Aonghasa, at a redshift of 8.13, seen as it was about 630 million years after the Big Bang.

Which telescopes found it?

Euclid first identified it. Keck, Hubble, the Large Binocular Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope confirmed it and measured its redshift.

How massive is its black hole?

Several hundred million times the mass of the Sun, according to the research team.

Why is it surprising?

It is hard to explain how a black hole grew so large so soon after the Big Bang without very rapid growth or a large starting seed.

What does it tell us about black hole origins?

The team found it consistent with "direct collapse," in which a gas cloud collapses directly into a large black hole seed.
